passage:
The science model was due on Monday, and it was Thursday. Sarita opened the box of clay, looked at it, and closed it again. "I do better when the clock is running out," she told Mehak on the call. "And I'll start right after one more video." One video became five. On Saturday she said the room was too messy to think. On Sunday she said she would wake up early instead.
What she did not say aloud was the small cold thought underneath: if she tried properly and it still looked poor, everyone would see she was not clever. A rushed model at least came with an excuse ready. On Sunday night she finally slapped clay onto a board, and the volcano leaned and cracked as it dried. Tushar Sir held it up on Monday and asked where the crater had gone. Sarita shrugged and said she had not had time. Mehak noticed her thumbnail was chewed down to the skin.

qa.q: On which day was the science model due, and which day did Sarita open the clay box?
qa.a: The model was due on Monday, and Sarita opened the box of clay on Thursday.

qa.q: How do Sarita's excuses connect to the poor model she handed in?
qa.a: Her reasons, such as working better under pressure, waiting for one more video and a messy room, sounded fair, but under them was a fear that a properly tried model would reveal weakness. The delay protected her self-image, and it left a rushed volcano that cracked.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when she said she had not had time?
qa.a: She was ashamed and afraid of being judged. The chewed thumbnail and the shrug suggest she was hiding how much it worried her.

qa.q: What small step could Sarita take next time a project feels scary?
qa.a: She could start with ten minutes of rough work on day one and show it to Mehak or Tushar Sir early, so the first attempt is allowed to be imperfect.

grounding: A teen's reasonable-sounding excuses (3188) serve to avoid judgement and protect self-image (4056), and the delay makes the work worse.
